analytic.title: Worst-Case Response Time Analysis for OSEK/VDX Compliant Real-time Distributed Control Systems

div.p: Temporal behaviors prediction is very critical for real-time control systems. This paper presents a method to analysis the worst-case response time of OSEK/VDX compliant hard real-time distributed control systems. OSEK/VDX is an industry standard for an open-ended architecture for distributed control units in vehicles. Traditional time analysis methods based on the fixed priority preemptive scheduling model do not account for the problems occur in practical systems. Based on the current time analysis technologies, we propose an accurate time analysis method considering the practical effects of resource access synchronization, mixed preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling, as well as the overheads of OSEK OS. Furthermore, we also propose a scheme to efficiently integrate time analysis tools into the current development process for electronic control units in vehicles.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: OSEK/VDX [1] is an industry standard for an openended architecture for distributed control units in vehicles. A real-time operating system, software interfaces and functions for communication and network management tasks are specified in this standard. All the big-name companies in the automobile industry support OSEK/VDX and there is a task force that is working on an ISO standardization of OSEK/VDX. For simplicity OSEK will be used instead of OSEK/VDX in this paper.

In hard real-time distributed control systems, jobs have stringent timing constraints and often require to be executed on a sequence of processors. Timing constraints are typically given in form of end-to-end deadline. A job in such a system meets its timing constraint if it completes before its end-to-end deadline. If one or more jobs miss their deadlines, the results are unexpected and can be catastrophic, leading to loss of life and/or property. In order to verify that a given control hardware and software system is capable of providing the required quality of control, a means of predicting end-to-end response times is required. Preferably, this information should be available at an early design stage.

Most of real-time control systems are scheduled using fixed priorities, and thus Rate Monotonic analysis (RMA) [2] [3] is used. Although most of the RMA theory is devoted to single-processor systems, the RMA techniques can also be applied to distributed systems [4] [5] by modeling each network as if it were a processor and each message as if it were a task. These techniques can accurately predict the worst-case end-to-end response times in real-time distributed control systems under an ideal condition such as, the interrupt service routines (ISRs) and tasks are entirely coincide with the fixed priorities scheduling model. However, these methods didn't consider the problems might occur when being applied to practical systems. For example, the task set of an OSEK compliant OS [6] may mix preemptable tasks and non-preemptable tasks. This type of systems cannot be treated as preemptive scheduling model. Thus RMA techniques can not adapt to these cases any more.

This paper focuses on the worst-case end-to-end response time analysis of OSEK compliant hard realtime distributed control systems. In these systems we assume that electronic control units (ECUs) communicate using the Controller Area Network (CAN) field bus. We improve the traditional RMA to deal with the practical response time analysis of systems based on the OSEK standard and also propose a strategy to integrate time analysis into the development process of ECUs in vehicles. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the established analysis of task and message scheduling for computing worst-case bounds on response times. Section 3 presents a complementary time analysis of worst-case bounds for OSEK compliant single-processor. Section 4 provides a method to integrate automatic time analysis into development of ECUs. Finally, we conclude our paper and describe a program of further work in section 5.

div.head: Current analysis technique
div.p: In a distributed system there are several processor resources (ECUs) and one or more communication resources (CAN field buses). We shall assume preemptive scheduling based on fixed priorities, in order to be able to use RMA for the analysis of the worst-case timing behavior of both tasks and messages. We can regard ISRs as tasks with periods equal to their minimum inter-arrival time. We will also assume a realtime communications system that uses priority preemptive scheduling, and thus we will treat the messages in the communication resources in the same way as the tasks in the processors resources, except for a small blocking term that must be taken into account because the message are composed of sequences of packets, each of which is indivisible and non preemptive.

One approach that can be used is to analyze each processing and communication resource of the system as if it was independent [7]. The analysis is partitioned into components that can be individually analyzed. With the negotiation between nodes and network implementers, the agreed deadlines place contractual requirements on each component, the analysis of which can be carried out using the normal RMA techniques [8]. When all contracts are satisfied, the overall deadline is guaranteed. This approach is simple and can be easily implemented. But the contacts between components are difficult to determine. Improper contacts will lead to highly pessimistic analysis results. Moreover, it does not take into account the effects of jitter or deferred activation. In distributed systems the messages are activated by the execution of the tasks, and their activation instants are not perfectly periodic, but depend on the completion time of the triggering task, which is variable. Exactly the same happens with the tasks activated by the arrival of messages.

The solution to this problem was proposed by Tindell and Clark [4] and consists of repeating the worst-case analysis iteratively (calculation of repeating the worst-case analysis and jitter for all the system's resources) starting with jitter values equal to zero. The monotonic dependency of the response time with respect to jitter makes the analysis converge to a stable solution.

Periodic system transactions are defined as precedence constrained tasks and messages that are executed in sequence. To achieve accurate worst-case response time analysis for OSEK compliant control systems, in the next section, we analyze the characters of OSEK OS relevant to temporal behaviors and improve the established algorithms to deal with the issue of tasks synchronization, mixed preemptive scheduling and effects of overheads in OSEK OS.

div.head: Time analysis for OSEK compliant single-processor systems
div.p: The specification of the OSEK OS [6] is to represent a uniform environment, which supports efficient utilization of resource for automobile control unit application software. The OSEK OS is a single processor operating system meant for distributed embedded control units. It serves as a basis for application programs, which are independent of each other, and provides their environment on a processor. The OSEK operating system enables a controlled realtime execution of several processes, which appear to run in parallel. OSEK defines three processing levels: interrupt level, logical level for scheduler and task level. Within the task level tasks are scheduled (none, full or mixed preemptive scheduling) according to their user assigned priority. Interrupts have precedence over tasks. The interrupt processing level consists of one or more interrupt priority levels. Users statically assign the priority for ISRs and tasks.

OSEK OS features are described as four conformance classes: BCC1, BCC2, ECC1, ECC2 according the attributes: multiple requesting of task activation, task types, and number of tasks per priority. In this paper, BCC1 class is assumed, since it can meet the requirements of most real-time control systems in vehicles. For this class, only basic tasks are supported, the OS is limited to one activation request per task and one task per priority, while all tasks have different priorities.

For flexibility and performance considerations, OSEK OS supports mixed preemptive scheduling. In this case the scheduling policy depends on the preemption properties of the running task. If the running task is non-preemptable, then non-preemptive scheduling is performed. If the running task is preemptable, then preemptive scheduling is performed. This is quite different from the basic assumption of traditional time analysis methods. In addition, the resource access protocols and the overheads of OSEK OS should also be considered when analyzing a practical real-time system.

div.head: Time analysis for mixed preemptive scheduling
div.p: The OSEK OS supports full preemptive scheduling, non-preemptive scheduling and mixed preemptive scheduling for flexibility and performance considerations. This increases the complexity of time analysis. Full preemptive scheduling and nonpreemptive scheduling can be regarded as special cases of mixed preemptive scheduling with zero preemptive tasks or zero non-preemptive tasks. Therefore, we only need to analyze the case of mixed preemptive scheduling. To simplify this work, we analyze the temporal behaviors of ISRs, preemptable tasks and nonpreemptable tasks respectively since they have distinct scheduling characters. According to equation ( 8), the response time of an action consists of three portions. The WCET C i can be obtained by testing or analyzing the code and this is not our focus. We will concentrate on the calculations of I i and B i .

In the case of mixed preemptive scheduling, ISRs can preempt any tasks either preemptable or not. For an ISR i , accessing resources occupied by tasks or ISRs with lower priority will block its execution. Therefore, its blocking time B i , can be computed through equation (9). Combining the methods proposed by [4] and [12], we achieve a practical worst-case response time analysis method for OSEK compliant hard real-time distributed control systems in automobiles. Besides the scheduling policies, the overhead of the operating system is another factor has to be taken into account for accurate time analysis.

div.head: Effects from the overhead of OSEK OS
div.p: Operating systems support concurrent executions of tasks, which can effectively improve the utilization of the processor. However, the OS itself occupies a portion of resources, even if the proportion is much smaller than the execution time of tasks and ISRs. To achieve accurate analysis results, we have to clarify which overheads of OSEK OS should be considered and how they contribute to the calculation of worst-case response time. The OSEK OS standard require OS vendor to provide a list of parameters specifying the implementation in functionality, performance and memory demand. Furthermore the basic conditions to reproduce the measurement of those parameters. Table I lists the performance parameters relevant to response time analysis. The listed performance parameters are determinate for a given operating system and hardware. Interrupts handling performance can be obtained directly from the datasheet of hardware. Other parameters relevant to scheduling can be achieved by testing or analyzing code running on specific hardware. Although application developers are usually not aware of these overheads, they will indeed contribute to the response time of control systems. To simplify the calculation, we can treat these overheads as contributions to the WCET or blocking time of tasks and ISRs as shown in the third column of table 1.

div.head: Integration of time analysis in control systems development
div.p: Response time analysis can predict the time behaviors of real-time distributed control systems before they are deployed in practical environments. This is critical for the safety-critical control systems. Time analysis tools are preferred to be used in design stage of these systems.

To reach the goal of OSEK of portable software, the OSEK Implementation Language (OIL) [16] has been defined to describe the configuration of an application using OSEK. This specification only addresses a single CPU in an ECU, not an ECU network. This means for each CPU there is only one OIL description. All OSEK system objects are described using OIL objects. The OIL description of the OSEK application is considered to be composed of a set of OIL objects. Based on the description, OSEK standard also gives an example of development process for applications [16].

Each objects defined in OIL is described by a set of attributes and references. Some of the objects and their attributes are relevant to response time analysis of an ECU, such as the number and priorities of ISRs and tasks. However, this information is not sufficient to accurately analysis the response time of an ECU. Another problem is that OIL cannot describe the topological architecture and channel characters of a distributed control system.

To solve these problems, developers have to provide additional information including temporal characters descriptions of the applications running on a single ECU, temporal and load characters descriptions of channels, and topological architecture description of the ECU network. Some of this information can be achieved at the beginning of the development process. With the advance of development process, more information is available, thus we can achieve a more accurate analysis result.

Figure 1 shows the scheme of integrating response time analysis into development process of control systems. Using a graphical or textual editor, users can produce three classes of configuration files: application configuration files for each ECU, a channels configuration file and an architecture configuration file for the whole distributed system.

The application configuration files contain the objects and their attributes specified by OIL. Since OIL cannot provide sufficient description of temporal characters, we add necessary temporal attributes to existing OIL objects. We call the extended specification Extended OSEK Implementation Language (EOIL). At least four additional attributes listed in table II must be added in EOIL. Based on EOIL, users will provide extended configuration files that contain necessary temporal information for each ECU. The channels configuration file describes the characters of each channel between ECUs. For each channel object, three attributes are specified: communication protocols, transmission speed and a list of messages transmitted in this channel. Based on the protocol attribute, a time analysis tool can choose specific model to calculate the worst-case transmission latency in the channel. All the message attributes are referred to the massage objects specified in the extended application configuration files of ECUs.

The architecture configuration file specifies the relationships between various resources (ECUs or channels) of a distributed ECU network. These relationships are defined in transactions, which are precedence-constrained tasks and messages executed in sequence. For each transaction object, this file specifies the tasks and messages composing it, as well as their precedence constraints. The tasks and messages are referred to corresponding objects in extended application configuration files.

The OS profile file provides the temporal performance parameters of the OSEK OS. Using the information provided by the four types of files mentioned above, a time analysis tool based on the time analysis algorithms introduced in this paper can accurately calculate worst-case response time for each transaction. The left portion of the dashed in Figure 1 is the existing development process for ECUs proposed by OSEK [16]. The right portion is the time analysis process suggested by this paper. Obviously, time analysis can be concurrently performed with the existing development process and can verify the system time behaviors in the whole design stage.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we introduce the method to analysis the worst-case response time of OSEK compliant hard real-time distributed control systems. Traditional time analysis methods for real-time control systems are usually based on the fixed priority preemptive scheduling model. OSEK OS is not perfectly consistent with this ideal model. Based on the current time analysis technologies, we propose an accurate time analysis method for control systems compliable with OSEK standard. This method considers the effects of resource access synchronization, mixed preemptive and nonpreemptive scheduling, and the overheads of OSEK OS. Besides, we also proposed a scheme to efficiently integrate time analysis tools into the development process for control systems in automobiles. By this means, we can efficiently verify the time behaviors of a control system in design stage. Our program of further work includes sensitivity analysis of hard real-time distributed control systems. Sensitivity analysis is important because the development and deployment of industrial control products exist in a changing environment. For example, customer demands and specifications, prices of raw materials, and employee and equipment availability, are difficult to estimate and subject to change. This greatly interests us to find a solution to solve his problems and efficiently assist the development and deployment of industrial control products.
